title: Inquest jury rules Anthony Divers death a homicide
subtitle: After nearly seven hours of deliberation jury members return with 13 recommendations for government and police agencies to consider.
article: An inquest jury has ruled the police-shooting death of Anthony Divers a homicide.
Under the Coroner's Act, this means the 36-year-old's death is the result of one person causing the death of another.
But, since it is not a criminal finding, no blame is attached to the person who caused the death - in this case Hamilton police Const. Nicholas Cercone, who shot and killed Divers on Sept. 30, 2016.

After deliberating for close to seven hours Wednesday, the jury also came back with 13 recommendations for government and police agencies to consider, including recommendations aimed at improving police training, mental health treatment and the treatment of psychiatric patients.
Another recommendation asked the Ministry of Education to provide psychoeducational testing to at-risk youth to help mitigate difficulties later in life.
The purpose of the inquest was to review how Divers died - that is, by homicide, suicide or some other means - and to make recommendations to help avoid another, similar death in the future.
Divers' sister Yvonne Alexander was pleased with the recommendations, saying "thanks to the jury," her brother's voice has been heard.
He was a person in crisis and was unarmed, she added.
The inquest on Wednesday heard submissions from lawyers representing the Coroner's office, Hamilton police, Divers' family and the officer who shot Divers.

Cercone was one of several officers looking for Divers following a 911 call from Divers' wife. She told police he had assaulted her, was high on drugs - likely crystal meth and fentanyl - and could be armed with a Glock pistol. Police were also aware Divers had a violent past and had been convicted of manslaughter.

Cercone found Divers on James Street South and planned to arrest him, but Divers did not comply with his orders not to move and a chase ensued. Divers slowed down but refused to show his hand, which was hidden under his shirt. Fearing Divers was holding a gun, Cercone fired two bullets, one of which hit Divers, when the latter took a step toward him. That was just before midnight on a busy Friday when the street was full of traffic, pedestrians and restaurant goers.
Divers was pronounced dead at St. Joseph's hospital at 12:25 a.m. on Oct. 1.
During submissions to the jury before its deliberations, lawyers for the Hamilton Police Service and the officer who shot Divers urged the jury to find the 36-year-old died by suicide.
The inquest heard evidence that Divers attempted suicide and had been suicidal on several occasions in the past. It also heard he had been hospitalized for mental health issues.

A few witnesses made reference to the possibility of the shooting being a "suicide by cop" situation. "Suicide by cop" is a term used to describe an incident when a suicidal person deliberately engages in threatening behaviour in order to provoke a lethal response from police.
The SIU, which investigates police shootings, in 2017 cleared Cercone and found he was justified in his actions.
Roy Wellington, lawyer for the Divers family, told the jury he rejected the idea that Divers could have died of suicide that night.
"Anthony Divers died as a result of officer Cercone's intentional use of force," he said.
He also rejected the idea that what happened was a confluence of events, and that there was nothing else that could be done.
"We heard he had plans to go out west the following week," Wellington said.
Though the possibility of "suicide by cop" was mentioned during the inquest, Coroner John Carlisle advised the jury that it cannot be deemed a cause of death under the Coroner's Act.

There was also much said about police training and the use-of-force model used by the Ontario Police College, with police training experts testifying and explaining the type of training officers get at the college and through local police services. The use of force model used in Ontario dates back to 2004 and is currently being updated.
